segments.text: For most things, you just open up your AI app, type in a quick question, and keep the conversation moving.
But then you hit a task that asks a lot more.
You might be staring down a complicated plan or weighing a dozen different options.
Or maybe you need to pull together a deep investigation,
cross-referencing facts from a bunch of different sources without losing the thread.
When that happens, you need to step away from the default settings.
Depending on the app you're using and your subscription tier,
you actually have three advanced levers you can pull.
Those levers are the model, the thinking time, and the research mode.
You don't need to touch these for every single prompt,
but knowing exactly when to switch them on is how you get AI to stop giving you generic text
and start doing actual heavy lifting work.
Whether you use ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, the answers are powered by a large language model, or LLM.
You can think of that LLM as the actual engine sitting under the hood of the app.
So when you see a dropdown menu that lets you choose a model,
what you're really doing is selecting which engine you want to engage.
It is best to leave this on the default setting as your baseline for standard day-to-day use.
But different models have different capability ceilings.
When a prompt gets too heavy for the base engine, it's time to upgrade.
This board lays out the choice between an everyday model and a more capable model.
The everyday model is built for quick questions and simple tasks.
For instance, suggest a funny movie to watch tonight.
The more capable model steps in for demanding tasks with details to work through.
If you're asking it to help me plan a summer business,
including costs, pricing, and how many customers I'll need, that requires higher logic.
You upgrade the model when your prompt moves away from simple lookups
and turns into a multifaceted scenario with variables and business logic.
Choosing a model changes the engine,
but activating the thinking feature changes how long that engine is allowed to run.
Now, the AI isn't actually thinking the way you or I do.
What it's doing is spending more computational time
working through the prompt before it hands you the final output.
This board shows how allocating time changes the output,
splitting tasks into less thinking and more thinking.
With less thinking, the AI spends little time processing, which is fine for routine work.
If you need it to turn these nodes from our group meeting into a clear checklist,
it can do that almost instantly.
But with more thinking, the AI takes extra time to weigh options and check answers.
You want this for deep analysis,
like asking it to help us divide this project among four people with different schedules.
The AI needs time to balance constraints.
Turning up the thinking time is a deliberate trade-off.
You are sacrificing immediate speed so you can get a verified multi-step result.
Then there's the third option, research.
This focuses on pulling in external information that sits outside of the AI space training data.
This mode actively goes out, gathers data from various websites,
and brings it all back so you can compare your options side by side.
Regular chat can look things up on the internet too,
but research is built for a much fuller cross-referenced investigation.
This graphic compares regular chat on the left and deep research on the right.
Use regular chat for direct answers to logistical questions,
like asking,
How long would it take me to drive from Dallas to Texas A&M in College Station vs. UT Austin?
Deep research expands the mandate.
It extracts information from dozens of sites, compares them, and builds a report showing sources.
If you ask it to compare the physics program that Texas A&M and UT Austin,
including undergraduate research, admissions, and costs, and show your sources,
it does the heavy lifting.
Deep research is essential when a quick, factual retrieval isn't enough.
And you need a fully verified landscape of information.
For the vast majority of your low-stakes, everyday questions,
those default settings are going to work perfectly fine.
But the moment you move from a simple chat to a complex execution,
you have to consciously choose to activate these advanced settings.
This banner lays out your consolidated checklist.
Model. Thinking. Research.
Use them when the work demands more.
Matching the exact capability of the tool to the complexity of the task
is what separates a casual user from an advanced one.
